meta.ogDescription: Not Socrates. It paraphrases Kenneth John Freeman's 1907 dissertation Schools of Hellas — his own summary of ancient grumbles, never a quote of Socrates.

answer.label: Not Socrates — written by Kenneth John Freeman (1907)
answer.authorDates: 1882–1906 · Cambridge classical scholar; dissertation published posthumously 1907
answer.sourceLine: The words are a modern paraphrase of a passage in Kenneth John Freeman’s Cambridge dissertation Schools of Hellas (1907), p. 74 — Freeman’s OWN summary of the complaints Athenians of Socrates’ day levelled at the young, not a quotation of Socrates. Freeman actually wrote: “The counts of the indictment are luxury, bad manners, contempt for authority, disrespect to elders, and a love for chatter in place of exercise.” No such passage appears in Plato, Xenophon, or any ancient source. As Quote Investigator documents, the line was pinned on Socrates by 1922.

source.excerpt: The counts of the indictment are luxury, bad manners, contempt for authority, disrespect to elders, and a love for chatter in place of exercise. Children began to be the tyrants, not the slaves, of their households.
source.trailTitle: How a 1907 paraphrase became a 'Socrates quote'
trail: 1907: Kenneth John Freeman writes the passage in Schools of Hellas (p. 74) as his own summary of ancient grievances — the full text is on Project Gutenberg and Internet Archive.
1922: the Oakland Tribune reattaches the words to Socrates, per Quote Investigator.
Verdict: classicists agree it is a fake Socrates quotation — no such line exists in any ancient text.
source.excerptNote: Freeman's actual 1907 wording (as documented by Quote Investigator). The familiar “The children now love luxury…” version is a later paraphrase that recast his prose into a first-person ‘quotation.’

source.rightsNote: The underlying passage — Freeman's Schools of Hellas (1907) — is itself long in the public domain (published well before 1931). But the popular first-person wording (“The children now love luxury…”) is not Freeman's text; it is an anonymous 20th-century paraphrase whose exact phrasing evolved through newspapers, so the specific wording shown here has no single identifiable, datable source. We therefore mark the status uncertain rather than claim public-domain for a line no one is documented to have authored in this form.

author.name: Kenneth John Freeman
author.heading: About Kenneth John Freeman
author.metaLine: 1882–1906 · Cambridge classicist · author of Schools of Hellas (1907)
author.bio: Kenneth John Freeman was a young Cambridge classical scholar whose dissertation, Schools of Hellas: An Essay on the Practice and Theory of Ancient Greek Education from 600 to 300 B.C., was published posthumously in 1907 (edited by M. J. Rendall, with a preface by A. W. Verrall). On page 74 he paraphrased the standard ancient grumbles about badly-behaved youth to give readers the flavour of the era. He never presented the lines as a quotation — and certainly not as the words of Socrates. Decades of newspapers turned his summary into a fake ‘Socrates said’ quotation.

misattribution.heading: A fake Socrates quotation
misattribution.intro: This is one of the internet’s most persistent fake ‘ancient wisdom’ quotes. The thought is real 20th-century scholarship; the Socrates label is an error.

items.why: Attributed to Socrates on countless quote sites and social posts, but no such passage exists in Plato, Xenophon, or any text preserving Socrates’ words. Quote Investigator shows it was pinned to Socrates only in 1922.
Occasionally credited to Plato because Freeman’s passage broadly evokes Plato’s Republic, but Freeman was summarising, not quoting — the words are his, per Kiwi Hellenist.

Even the ‘real’ text is paraphrased: Freeman wrote “The counts of the indictment are luxury, bad manners, contempt for authority, disrespect to elders, and a love for chatter in place of exercise” — later recast into the smoother first-person ‘quotation’ seen today.

misattribution.truthLine: The true author is Cambridge scholar Kenneth John Freeman, writing in Schools of Hellas (1907) — his own summary of ancient grumbles, never the words of Socrates (Quote Investigator).

context.heading: Why it spread
lead: The quote endures because it flatters a comforting idea: that adults have complained about ‘kids these days’ since antiquity, so today’s worries are nothing new. Freeman’s 1907 passage genuinely captured that ancient sentiment — which is exactly why it was so easy to mistake his summary for an actual ancient voice.

Once a 1922 newspaper attached the name ‘Socrates,’ the borrowed authority made the line irresistible. Even Malcolm Forbes’ magazine tried and failed to trace it in the 1960s, and it still circulates as gospel today.
context.pull: An authentic idea about the ancient world — wearing a fake ancient name.
